q: The base's confirmation e-mail reminds you to bring your papers to check-in. What goes in your hand luggage?

Your logbook and the sailing-school certificates of each crew member
The boat's registration and insurance, printed from the base's website

Yes, but you will write him on the list yourself when he arrives
No — the list is for the people who signed the charter contract
why: Everyone who sleeps aboard is on the crew list; a change mid-week is reported to the base, which amends the list for the port police.

q: Reading the deposit clause, your crew ask what it costs if the dinghy flips and the outboard goes to the bottom. What do you tell them?

o: At most the deposit — that is exactly what the deposit is for
Nothing — the boat's insurance covers the tender and its motor
Half the price — the base shares losses that are nobody's fault
why: The deposit caps insured damage only; the contract lists what is charged in full — negligence, grounding, the dinghy and outboard.

lines: Held on card or in cash at check-in

It covers the hull only; everything else comes off the full deposit
It is the boat's insurance; without it the base cannot let you sail

o: At the base — the originals are too valuable to take to sea
In your bag, to show at the desk when you hand the boat back
At the marina office of your first harbour, with the crew list

Go by day only — the clause forbids night sailing, not the crossing
Go — the limits bind the boat's insurer, not the skipper

Leave under engine only — the wind limit is about sailing, not motoring
Leave on Friday at dawn instead; one day of F7 is a smaller risk than two

Photograph the wall chart and work out the details at sea
Note the no-go areas only; the rest is local colour

Accept, and read the owner's manual aboard tonight instead
Accept, but ask for the briefing on paper to read on passage

Wait for the base to call before leaving harbour each day
Look at the sky and the barometer; forecasts are for open-sea crossings
why: The briefing names the forecasts the base trusts for its area; the daily decision to sail starts with them.

o: The unused day is refunded at the daily rate
You must stay out until the return time in the contract
The deposit is reduced by one day's charter
why: Coming back early is your call and costs nothing extra; unused days are not refunded; call the base so a berth is free.

Fine, if you leave the bay at 06:00 and refuel on the way in
Fine — the base can check the boat out in the bay if you call them
why: The contract wants the boat back the evening before: the base checks her out, refuels and cleans her before the next crew.

lines: Boat in base marina: Friday by 18:00
Late return: a penalty per hour, plus costs

q: The technician fills in the form as you walk round and hands it to you to sign. What do you do before you sign?
a: Read every line against what you saw, add what is missing, then photograph the form and the boat
o: Sign — the technician's copy is the one that counts and he has written it all down
Sign, and photograph the boat later in the evening when it is quieter
Sign, and e-mail the base a list of everything else you can remember
why: The check-in form is what the deposit is settled against; anything not on it counts as new damage at check-out.

q: Your partner also holds a licence and will skipper half the week. The contract looks like this. What do you do?
a: Have the base add them as co-skipper now, licence shown, before the contract is signed
o: Nothing — once the skipper is checked, anyone aboard may take the helm
Add their name to the crew list and leave the contract as it is
Carry their licence aboard and show it only if the port police ask

q: At the office the desk asks you to sign the contract and the check-in form together, 'the technician will walk you round afterwards'. What do you do?
a: Sign the contract; the check-in form only after the walk-round, with what you found on it
o: Sign both — the walk-round is a formality and the form can be amended by e-mail
Sign neither until the technician has walked you round the boat
Sign both, and photograph the boat so that you have your own record
why: The check-in form records the state of the boat as you took her over; it is signed after the walk-round, not before.

q: It is 19:30 on Saturday, the base is handing over twelve boats, and the technician says 'she's fine, sign here, I'll come by tomorrow if anything is wrong'. What do you do?
a: Walk round yourself now, write what you find on the form, and have the base countersign it tonight
o: Sign — he has seen the boat, and you will phone the base about anything tomorrow
Refuse to sign, sleep ashore and come back on Sunday morning when it is quieter
Sign now, then e-mail the base a list of defects first thing on Sunday

C — the visitor quay for the night; the return berth is for Saturday
B — berth; the base's refuelling costs the same as the pontoon
why: Full to full: the boat comes back with full tanks; refuelling by the base is charged on top of the fuel.

Open the windlass and repair it yourselves so that nothing is charged
Sail on to the next big harbour and find a mechanic there yourselves
why: Under the contract the skipper reports a fault at once and does not carry on with it; the base decides the repair.

Let him go, and have the pulpit straightened at the yard here today
Take the cash and write the damage on the check-out form on Friday

The charter contract — it shows that the base is responsible for the boat
A photo of the papers on your phone; the originals stay at the base
why: Port police check the transit log and crew list against the registration and insurance; they must be aboard and current.

q: The desk takes an imprint of your card for the deposit and your crew say €3,000 has just left your account and want to split it tonight. What do you tell them?

o: It has — the base charges the deposit now and repays it in cash at check-out
It has — the deposit is charged now and refunded by bank transfer the week after
Nothing has left: the base keeps the card number and charges only if something breaks

q: Reading the deposit clause at the desk, you realise your card will not cover it. What do you do?
a: Put a second card up for the rest, or pay the balance in cash against a receipt
o: Leave your passport with the base as security for the difference
Sign now and bring the rest on Monday, once your bank has raised the limit
Ask the base to hold €2,000 now and take the rest on your co-skipper's word

o: They are right — the excess is the ceiling for the week, whatever else happens
They are wrong the other way: two incidents in a week cancel the waiver altogether
They are right, but the base will want a new €500 before you may leave harbour
why: A waiver's excess is charged on each incident unless the contract says otherwise; two incidents mean two excesses.

fig.title: Waiver — the excess

q: Your crew ask whether the boat's insurance covers their injuries and luggage. What do you tell them?
a: No — the policy covers the boat and third parties; each of you needs travel insurance that covers sailing
o: Yes — everyone on the crew list is insured under the boat's policy
Yes, for injuries aboard; luggage is covered out of the deposit
No one is covered; that is what the deposit is for
why: A yacht's policy insures the hull and liability to others; crew injury, luggage and cancellation are the charterer's own travel insurance.

q: Your crew ask whether, if one of them is at the helm when the boat hits a quay, that person pays the deposit. What do you tell them?
a: No — the skipper named in the contract answers to the base for any damage; how you share it is between you
o: Yes — the base charges whoever was at the helm, so everyone should keep their card handy
Yes — that is why each crew member signs the contract at check-in
No — damage with a crew member at the helm is the base's risk, not the charterer's
why: The contract makes the named skipper responsible for the boat and crew; the base settles the deposit with the skipper, not with the helmsman.

o: Yes — a club regatta is sailing in company, which is cruising, not racing
Yes, if you enter the cruising class and pay the entry fee yourselves
Yes, if you sail under mainsail alone and keep clear of the marks
why: Racing is excluded from the charter and from its insurance; only the base's written consent could change that.

Yes, if he signs a note that he sails at his own risk
Yes, if you call the base before you leave the quay and give his name

lines: Lefkas, Monday: a friend asks to join for the day

o: Children under 12 sail free and the base needs the ages for the invoice
The base needs the ages for the crew list; children are not counted as persons aboard
So the base can fit cots; children are not entered on the crew list
why: Children are crew: on the crew list, within the persons limit, and in a lifejacket of the right size, which the base supplies.

q: Your crew want to bring the dog for the week. What do you do?

o: Bring it — a small dog is not a pet in the sense of the contract
Bring it and tell the technician on the pontoon; the fee is settled at check-out
Bring it, but leave it off the crew list so the port police need not know

o: Tow her — the duty to help at sea overrides any clause in a charter contract
Tow her, once her skipper has signed a note accepting any damage to either boat
Sail on — the clause means you may not even stop for a boat that is not in distress

Stay out and beat to the base; the clause is absolute and the fine is worse than F7

Press on and call the base from the quay so that they know you arrived safely

Take A — the attendant knows his harbour better than the base does

Pass inshore of the inner flag — nets are set to seaward of their flags

Anchor at A and move to B if the gusts come; it is only across the bay

Sail until the wind reaches 6, then look for shelter — that is what the wind limit means
Stay in the bay you are in; it has been calm since Monday

Let them go and give them the base's briefing sheet to read on Sunday
Insist they all stay — the base will not sign off the briefing otherwise

Photograph the phone list and hand the pack back; it is heavy and not yours
Read the harbour notes once you are in the first harbour and need them

Ch 16 — the coast guard will pass the message on to the base

Sail as planned — the licence is checked at the base, not at sea
Ask the base to write 'renewal pending' on the contract and renew it online from the boat

o: Yourself — the ship's radio licence covers whoever is at the set
Nobody — the VHF is for emergencies, and anyone may call MAYDAY
Nobody — then the base must take the VHF off the inventory
why: The ship's licence covers the set; the operator needs a certificate, and the base files the certificated crew member as operator.

Nothing — the base refunds harbour fees against the receipts you bring back
Only the marinas; town quays are free to charter yachts

Nothing — the tax is for private yachts, not for charter boats
Your card — the tax is paid by the crew in the first port of call

o: Do — an empty bottle on return is charged, whatever the policy says

End in Corfu as agreed and leave the boat on the visitor quay with the keys at the office
Finish in Lefkas and pay the base the Corfu berth fee you saved

Nothing — sleep aboard and leave at dawn; the briefing is for first-time charterers
Ask to sign the check-in form by e-mail on Saturday so that Sunday is yours

o: The saloon and the cabins — the hull is the base's business, not yours

The form only — the technician photographs the boat for the base's file
